title: Rory McIlroy relishing battle for Harry Vardon Trophy in Dubai - Articles - Rolex Series
article_text:
Rory McIlroy is raring to go in his bid to chase down Eugenio Chacarra and win a record-equalling eighth Harry Vardon Trophy which will come down to the wire at next week's DP World Tour Championship.

The World Number Two leapfrogged long-time leader of the Race to Dubai Rankings Delivered by DP World Patrick Reed into second after adding a third-placed finish at the 2026 Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship.

He trails Chacarra by 533.93 points heading into the final event of the season on the Earth course, where the six-time Major Champion has won on three occasions, and with 2,000 points on offer for the winner, McIlroy is relishing the chance to sit alongside Colin Montgomerie in the record books.

"It was a good week. I saw some encouraging signs in the game," the 37-year-old said.

"I'm going to be in that final group going out on Thursday next week. I obviously would have loved to have won the tournament, but enough positive signs to feel good about going into next week.

"That's where I wanted to be. It's a pretty familiar spot for me going into the DP World Tour Championship and I'm excited for it.

"That was the goal coming into these two weeks to try to catch Eugenio and Patrick, and try to win the Race to Dubai again.

"It would have been great to win this week and give myself not as much of a deficit or even a lead, but still feel like I'm right in there with a great chance."

Chacarra declared McIlroy as the favourite despite his advantage heading into Dubai.

"It's hard. He's the number two player in the world and the number one in Europe, and he's been doing it for a long time and he plays really good out in Abu Dhabi and Dubai," the Spaniard admitted.

"He has played that course a million times, and I only played it once.

"He's going to be up there and we are going to battle on next week. Obviously the odds are on him and he's the favourite, but we'll play golf.

"We know what I'm capable of when I am playing good. There was a lot of good this week, but I just need to sharpen up to have a chance next week."

Jon Rahm stormed to victory at Yas Links on his tournament debut to give himself with a shot of winning his second Race to Dubai crown and his first since 2019.

The Spaniard would need Chacarra to finish no higher than eighth and McIlroy as runner-up should he secure succesive triumphs to conclude the season in his outside chance of lifting the Harry Vardon Trophy.

He said: "I didn't think I ever had a chance to win it! I'm very excited, it gives me a little more incentive for next week because I really didn't think I had a chance.

"Those are better odds than I expected so I'm looking forward to it and hopefully I can get my fourth one (victory on Earth course) and finish the year with back-to-back wins."

title: Korea Open: Indomitable An Equals Greatest Season
article_text:
A well deserved crown on her head, An Se Young has matched her own greatest season. Her win at the YEOSU VICTOR Korea Open 2026 is her 11th title of the year, equalling the tally she set in 2025 and leaving her one crown away from a new benchmark for the most titles won in a single year across all badminton disciplines. A remarkable achievement.

And she did it in style on home soil. A rare appearance in front of a packed Jinnam Stadium in Yeosu became a celebration as two titans of the sport went head-to-head when An outlasted Akane Yamaguchi 21-12 15-21 21-16 to seal the title.

There was little between the two rivals who have played each other a staggering 40 times, but throughout the final, it demanded An’s full attention. Yamaguchi’s trademark movement, shot variation and ability to change the rhythm of rallies ensured the Korean audience of a tasty final.

“Even when I had match point, Yamaguchi is someone who can close the gap. I tried to keep the intensity up until the very last point,” An told BWF post-match, smiling.

An arrived at the final having lost to Japanese shuttler at the Korea Open final last year (but An has now won the last 11 matches in a row), said she never allowed previous meetings to influence her mindset.

“I don’t let past results intimidate me. Sometimes I win and sometimes she wins. I didn’t think too much about last year.”

Against a player capable of producing something different in each rally, An knew there would be no opportunity to relax.

Yamaguchi’s unpredictability was a major test, with the Korean shuttler admitting before the match that reading her opponent would be one of the biggest challenges. That proved true throughout a match that demanded patience and discipline.

Opportunities to compete in front of home fans remain relatively rare for An, and the atmosphere in Yeosu was electric.

“There aren’t many matches for me in Korea, so it feels like a dream. A lot of fans were cheering for me, and I felt really proud. I can’t thank them enough. I’m glad and proud that so many Korean fans are supporting and enjoying badminton.”

For all her success, An believes the toughest matches remain the most important to her development.

“Against top players, I can’t have an easy match. I have to bring the intensity to the final point. They help me grow, and these kinds of matches make me a better, more stable player.”

title: WTA Finals Day 1 preview: Gauff, Pegula set for all-American battle at Indian Wells
article_text:
INDIAN WELLS, Calif. -- The 2026 FAGE WTA Finals at Indian Wells are set to begin Sunday, the 55th edition of the signature year-end event.

Following World No. 1 and defending champion Elena Rybakina's withdrawal, Marta Kostyuk enters the competition as first alternate.

Here’s an updated schedule for the opening day, followed by an in-depth preview of the singles matches.

12 p.m.:  [8] Linda Noskova vs. [ALT] [9] Marta Kostyuk

Followed by:  [4] Coco Gauff vs. [5] Jessica Pegula

Followed by:  [1] Katerina Siniakova/Taylor Townsend vs. [8] Sara Errani/Jasmine Paolini

Followed by:  [4] Cristina Bucsa/Nicole Melichar-Martinez vs. [6] Ellen Perez/Demi Schuurs

For the fourth time this season, Noskova and Kostyuk will go toe-to-toe to kick off the tournament. They've played each other on all three surfaces, with Noskova edging out Kostyuk 7-5, 5-7, 6-4 in their lone hard-court meeting at the US Open fourth round.

En route her Wimbledon championship, Noskova took the grass meeting in the semifinals, while Kostyuk won the battle on clay on her way to taking the Madrid title. Both of those matches were in straight sets.

"I feel like this year has definitely been a great buildup year, great buildup season for me," Noskova said in her pre-event press conference. "The results came my way. I was super excited about the grass season, also the clay season, and then the U.S. swing was great for me, as well."

Since that US Open encounter, Kostyuk has only managed to win one match since, her second round at Guadalajara. She last played on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz in Ningbo. As for Noskova, she last competed at the the Round of 16 in Beijing.

Both players have 35 wins in their 2026 season, and are making their debuts at the WTA Finals.

"Unbelievable season for me, and I never had a goal to end at WTA Finals," Kostyuk said. "Being here is obviously such a blessing, and I'm very excited to make my debut tomorrow. It's going to be great and exciting. The fact that it's happening in Indian Wells, I think, is also like a cherry on top, and it's great to be back here and play."

There is plenty of history between the friends and former doubles partners who have split their 10 meetings. The pair were drawn into the same group at last year's WTA Finals, where Dubai champion Pegula prevailed in three sets. But Cincinnati champion Gauff has won both of their 2026 encounters, in the Wimbledon quarterfinals and the Cincinnati final.

Gauff discussed that familiarity in her pre-event press conference, adding that it essentially becomes much more of a mental game, given they both know each other's play styles well.

"When you get to the point where you've played someone so many times, that's where it becomes really more difficult, just because of the fact that you got to capitalize on do things you do well, but also know they're going to change things, vice versa," Gauff said. "When you play somebody so many times, it becomes even more mental because you're both trying to figure out to go away from your own patterns, because they know your patterns."

Pegula reflected on both of their 2026 matchups in her press conference, recalling Gauff's high level in the final two sets at Wimbledon and from the start in Cincinnati. Still, it's a new matchup and things can change in an instant.

"You never know what's going to happen out there," Pegula said. "We know what we're going to try to do, try and change. We'll just see when we get out there if we're able to kind of execute what we want to. If one of us changes or is trying to do something different, how well we can react to that, as well. I think it will be interesting."

Overall, this marks the fourth consecutive year Gauff and Pegula have met at the year-end championships, with Pegula holding a 2-1 edge in their previous three matchups.

title: Race to Dubai: Rory McIlroy takes 'positive signs' into DP World Tour Championship after missing out on Abu Dhabi win
article_text:
Rory McIlroy insists there are ‘positive signs’ in his game going into the DP World Tour Championship, despite missing out on Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship victory.

McIlroy made a birdie-eagle start to his final round at Yas Links GC and held a share of the lead again with seven holes remaining, only to finish in third spot, four strokes behind Ryder Cup team-mate Jon Rahm.

He played the last seven holes of his three-under 69 in one over, seeing him end the week on 19 under, leaving McIlroy without a worldwide victory since successfully defending his title at The Masters in April.

"It was sort of a week where I felt like I had my chances," McIlroy admitted. "Especially today, birdieing 10 and 11 on the back nine to get tied for the lead. Then I had two good chances, 12 and 13, and didn't make those.

"Had to scramble for par on 14 and then I just couldn't keep my momentum going, but it was a good week. I saw some encouraging signs in the game."

McIlroy's third-place finish represents the 11th time he has come in the top three in 15 appearances in Abu Dhabi without victory, with the result lifting him above Patrick Reed into second in the Race to Dubai standings heading into the season finale.

The world No 2 now trails Eugenio Chacarra by 533.93 points going into the DP World Tour Championship, where 2,000 points are on offer for the winner and 1,335 points for second, with McIlroy challenging for a record-equalling eighth Order of Merit.

"I'm going to be in that final group going out on Thursday," McIlroy added. "I obviously would have loved to have won the tournament, but enough positive signs to feel good about going into next week.

"That [final group] is where I wanted to be. It's a pretty familiar spot for me going into the DP World Tour Championship, and I'm excited for it.

"That was the goal coming into these two weeks, to try to catch Eugenio [Chacarra] and Patrick [Reed] and try to win the Race to Dubai again.

"It would have been great to win this week and give myself not as much of a deficit, or even a lead, but still feel like I'm right in there with a great chance."

Chacarra has topped the standings since winning the DP World India Championship in October, his third victory of the season, with the Spaniard looking to find improvements in his game after failing to contend in Abu Dhabi.

"Drove the ball amazing the last two days and still made so many mistakes," Chacarra admitted. "A lot of little mistakes that got me out of being up there.

"My good was really good. I got a lot of birdies and hit really good long shots and made some good putts, but obviously I need to sharpen my short game and my wedges. It's a little frustrating because it's something we've been working on.

"Obviously the odds are on him [McIlroy] and he's the favourite, but we'll play golf. We know what I'm capable of when I am playing good. There was a lot of good this week, but I just need to sharpen the bat to have a chance next week."

Nine players still have a mathematical chance of winning the Race to Dubai, with Rahm now among those after an 11th DP World Tour title - his first since The Masters in 2023 and a record-breaking sixth Rolex Series victory.

"I didn't think I would ever have a chance to win it," admitted Rahm, who jumped to sixth in the standings. "Actually gives me a little extra incentive next week. Those are better odds than I expected so looking forward to it and hopefully I can get my fourth one [DP World Tour Championship]."

The DP World Tour season reaches its climax next week at the DP World Tour Championship, where only the top 50 available players in the Race to Dubai standings are eligible to compete.

title: DP World Tour season finale rocked by notable Ryder Cup absentees in Dubai
article_text:
European Ryder Cup heroes Matt Fitzpatrick and Shane Lowry are among the biggest names missing from this week's DP World Tour Championship after deciding against travelling to the Middle East.

Both players qualified for the season-ending tournament at Jumeirah Golf Estates but have opted not to make the trip to Dubai.

They are joined by Matt's younger brother Alex Fitzpatrick and Australian Min Woo Lee, who have also decided against travelling to the Middle East.

Lowry finished 20th in the Race to Dubai rankings, while Lee secured his place in 48th. Both players also bypassed last week's Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, the opening leg of the DP World Tour Playoffs.

Matt Fitzpatrick was 14th in the standings before Abu Dhabi, with Alex Fitzpatrik sitting 35th.

Concerns about travelling to the Middle East in November had already been raised by Matt Fitzpatrick during September's BMW PGA at Wentworth.

European Ryder Cup hero Ludvig Åberg is also another big name who will miss out on the season finale in Dubai.

The Swede slipped to 53rd in the Race to Dubai rankings, meaning he would have been in line to benefit from the four withdrawals and secure a place in Dubai.

However, Åberg, who also bypassed the Abu Dhabi Championship at Yas Links, has once again declined the opportunity to compete.

The withdrawals have allowed Ewen Ferguson, Matt Wallace, Victor Perez and Joost Luiten to move into the 50-man field instead.

Matt Fitzpatrick's absence will be particularly notable given his outstanding record at the tournament.

The former US Open champion has won the DP World Tour Championship three times, sharing the record with Rory McIlroy and Jon Rahm.

He has also enjoyed an excellent 2026 campaign, recording four victories around the world, while Alex has claimed two wins of his own.

Bob MacIntyre is another notable name missing from the DP World Tour Championship, although the Scot's circumstances are different.

MacIntyre was 56th in the Race to Dubai standings before the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, leaving him outside the top 50 and needing a strong result at Yas Links to qualify for the season finale.

However, his management team confirmed to GolfMagic last week that he would not travel to the Middle East also due to travel concerns.

By missing Abu Dhabi, MacIntyre also lost his final opportunity to climb into the qualifying positions and book his place in Dubai.

Justin Rose also decided to miss out on the first leg of the DP World Tour Playoffs in Abu Dhabi, which ruled him out of the DP World Tour Championship too.

The notable absences come amid attention on the security situation in the Middle East, with precautionary evacuation notices appearing around Yas Links during the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship.

The notices outlined the procedures players and caddies would need to follow in an emergency.

Play would be suspended immediately following an emergency mobile phone alert from UAE authorities, while a prolonged air horn blast would signal danger.

Players and caddies would then follow evacuation procedures and make their way to the clubhouse.

However, Rory McIlroy has insisted he has no concerns about competing in the region at the moment.

The Northern Irishman finished third in Abu Dhabi, moving from third to second in the Race to Dubai standings and keeping himself firmly in contention for another season-long title.

Speaking to reporters at Yas Links, McIlroy said: "I don't think I would ever feel unsafe.

"You know, even if something were to happen, like I still wouldn't feel unsafe.

"The UAE has great defence systems. Yeah, I think the only thing would be that if they closed the airspace and you were stuck here for a period of time, like people were at the start of year, but like I would still feel safe. I wouldn't feel like I would be in any danger."

McIlroy acknowledged that a potential airspace closure would be his main concern, but stressed that he was comfortable with the decision to compete.

"If everyone deems that it's safe to be here, then who am I to say otherwise?" he added.

"This is important to me. I want to play well. I want to end my year well. I wanted to have a chance to win another Race to Dubai.

"I don't feel like there's any risk coming here, but if I did feel like there was a risk, I feel like the reward is worth it."

While the likes of Fitzpatrick and Lowry will be absent, Rahm has given himself a major opportunity to finish the season on a high.

The Spaniard claimed a two-shot victory at the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, securing a record-breaking sixth Rolex Series title and his 11th DP World Tour victory.

It was also his first win on the DP World Tour since slipping on the famous Green Jacket at the 2023 Masters.

Rahm's latest win also transformed his Race to Dubai hopes, and gatecrashing McIlroy's record party in the process.

The former World No.1 climbed from 51st to sixth in the standings after collecting 1,500 points, putting himself in contention ahead of the final tournament.

Rahm admitted he had not expected to have a realistic chance of challenging for the season-long title.

"I didn't even think I'd have a chance to win it," he laughed.

"Yeah, I am very excited. It gives me a little extra incentive, I really didn't think I had a chance. I look forward to it."

title: How prize money and ranking points will be awarded at the 2026 WTA Finals
article_text:
The 2026 WTA Tour season is coming to a close, but for eight singles players there is one more task at hand: the WTA Finals in Indian Wells.

The tournament was dealt a significant blow on Saturday with Elena Rybakina, the year-end world No 1 and defending WTA Finals champion, forced to withdraw from the championships due to a viral illness.

However, action is still set to get underway to a strong start on Sunday, with Marta Kostyuk — Rybakina’s replacement — set to face Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova in the opening singles match, before 2024 WTA Finals champion Coco Gauff faces Jessica Pegula later in the day.

With Aryna Sabalenka, French Open champion Mirra Andreeva, Elina Svitolina, and Karolina Muchova also competing in Indian Wells, it promises to be a thrilling week of action in Tennis Paradise.

One of the most prestigious titles in tennis is at stake, and there are significant ranking points and prize money on offer.

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

Significant ranking points are on offer at the year-end championships, with a potential maximum of 1,500 points on offer for whoever triumphs in Indian Wells — the biggest number of points on offer outside of the four Grand Slam tournaments.

All eight singles players will start from scratch, with no points automatically awarded for qualifying.

Instead, 200 ranking points are on offer for each win during the round robin stage, meaning a player who wins all three matches would bank 600 ranking points ahead of the semi-final stage.

A record of two wins and one loss would earn a player 400 ranking points, a record of one win and two losses would earn 200 ranking points, while zero points would be awarded to a player who loses all three matches.

At the semi-final stage, the two players who reach the final will earn a further 400 ranking points for their victories in the last four, while the two beaten players will not earn any extra ranking points on top of their round robin winnings.

In the final, the eventual champion will earn a further 500 ranking points on top of the 400 ranking points earned for their semi-final win, and whatever they earned in across the round robin stage.

Any player who wins all three round robin matches, the semi-final, and then the final would take home a staggering 1,500 ranking points — just as Rybakina did in Riyadh last year.

A player with a 2-1 win-loss record in the round robin stage would take home 1,300 ranking points if they won the title, while a player with a 1-2 record would take home 1,100 points should they go on to win the title.

As revealed earlier this week, there is a total prize money pool of $10,000,000 across the singles and doubles events in Indian Wells this week, a notable decrease of 35.5% on the $15,250,000 on offer in Riyadh last season.

Unlike with ranking points, all eight players are ensured of prize money regardless of match wins, with a set participation fee of $220,000 for all the singles players.

However, each round robin match is then worth a further $230,000 per win, meaning a player who goes unbeaten in her group would earn a total of $690,000 on top of their participant fee of $220,000 — a total of $910,000 ahead of the semi-final stage.

The two victorious semi-finalists in the women’s singles draws will then take home a further $820,000 in prize money, with another $1,640,000 then awarded to whoever prevails in the final and lifts the title.

An unbeaten champion in Indian Wells would take home $3,3700,00 in prize money.

title: Jon Rahm's PGA Tour audition takes an interesting turn
article_text:
One of the nice things about being Jon Rahm is that your reputation precedes you.

You don’t need to provide your credentials to earn a tee time at the local club, or explain to the restaurant that you’d prefer a private table, or justify your desire to read your own putts to your caddie. You are Jon Rahm. Your resume speaks for itself.

As it turns out, that’s also why these few months are some of the weirdest of Rahm’s career. After LIV’s collapse, Rahm is suddenly auditioning for his pro career’s future, and hoping that a series of strong performances in the middle of the international fall season can help expedite his path back to the PGA Tour. And on Saturday evening in Abu Dhabi, Rahm’s resume means a little bit less than his spot on the 54-hole leaderboard: solo first.

First, the good news: Rahm can play on the DP World Tour as long as he likes. He has resolved his differences with the second-biggest men’s tour over fines stemming from his decision to leave for LIV in 2023 — and that deal clears his path to play there.

Second, the bad news: Rahm can’t play on the PGA Tour … at least not yet. The Tour hasn’t figured out a strategy for handling the throng of LIV players looking for a road back after the league’s dissolution, leaving that group in competitive limbo. In fact, according to a report from Gabby Herzig in The Athletic, the biggest men’s tour hasn’t even settled on an operating strategy yet — leaving open the possibility that the next few months’ worth of otherwise sleepy offseason golf could prove highly important in the shaping of public policy.

Enter: Jon Rahm. This week in Abu Dhabi, he’s back in the field for the first time since his attorneys informed the world he wouldn’t be playing on LIV any longer, following in the footsteps of fellow LIV pro Patrick Reed, who used the DP World Tour as a path back to the big tour. And what’s more? Rahm is playing well at Yas Links, entering Sunday’s final round with a one-shot lead atop a crowded leaderboard that includes Rory McIlroy, Tyrrell Hatton and Adam Scott.

A win on Sunday would give Rahm the rarest kind of golf treat: his first victory outside of LIV since the 2023 Masters. It couldn’t come at a better time, either. Should he win on Sunday in Abu Dhabi, Rahm would turn up the temperature on the conversation surrounding his PGA Tour return.

While Rahm’s play theoretically has no bearing on the Tour’s eventual decision — which won’t be decided until a bankruptcy court decides what to do with LIV’s outstanding player contracts — there’s little question that a prolonged hot streak for the former World No. 1 would be well-timed.

The Tour will have several factors to consider in an expedited reinstatement for players like Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau, but one of them will be the financial implication of saying “no.” A string of several consecutive starts in which Rahm looks indisputably like one of the five best players in the world would go a long way in helping his argument that the Tour stands to make more money with him than without him. A victory in an event against several of the best players in the world — like the opportunity that Rahm faces on Sunday morning — would help make the argument that the Tour’s competitive meritocracy and sense of stakes (two components of the future PGA Tour that commissioner Brian Rolapp has harped on) are better with Rahm in the field.

Of course, Rahm might not like the idea of “auditioning” for the PGA Tour. In a past life — like the one he was living 11 months ago — Rahm was given a special exemption to come back to the Tour with little penalty. But in this life, Rahm’s life has returned to the most elemental form of pro golf: You earn your opportunities with your play every single week.

On Sunday morning, Rahm could do himself plenty of good with another round of great golf. His reputation tells us a victory could be in our midst, but these days, the most important piece of Rahm’s reputation exists on the scorecard.

title: LIV Golf's end brought harsh answers to the sport's most pressing question
article_text:
Facing what would become golf’s biggest question, Xander Schauffele said he wasn’t sure where he stood. Jon Rahm’s attorney had just announced his client’s departure from LIV Golf, and Schauffele, one of the faces of the PGA Tour, was asked about a road back for defectors like Rahm. He didn’t divulge his feelings on the matter, but his explanation for the obstacles ahead once the LIV threat officially ended would prove prescient one month later.

“I’ve got no idea,” Schauffele said at the Baycurrent Classic last month. “There are 225 guys with Tour cards and if you sat down and interviewed all of them, you’re going to get probably three or four boxes of how guys feel. Some guys don’t care, some guys are really ticked off, some guys want them to have a huge fine, some guys would let them back tomorrow. Where I stand in those boxes, I don’t really know. I’m in the sort of, I try to mind my own business most times.”

One month later, LIV’s lawyers announced the league was entering the liquidation process of bankruptcy and that LIV 2.0 would not be happening as planned. As the rebel league went from existential threat to dust-covered relic, players in Abu Dhabi and Los Cabos were asked about a path back for Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau, Tyrrell Hatton and everyone in between. As Schauffele noted, the world of pro golf might be coming together, but opinions on its biggest question are divided.

Rory McIlroy and Justin Rose have said they’d welcome LIV defectors back. Scottie Scheffler said that “penalties” must be paid, but he would like “some” of the LIV guys back. At the World Wide Technology Championship, a player on the other end of the spectrum had a different opinion.

“Go back to Q-school,” Erik van Rooyen told Golfweek’s Adam Schupak in Mexico. “We were told initially that if you played LIV, you would be banned from the PGA Tour, and the story just kept changing. They gave the finger to the Tour. If you’re that good, go get it done.”

In Abu Dhabi, player director Adam Scott agreed that players who left should have to earn their way back to the tour they want to play on, be it the PGA Tour or the DP World Tour.

“I think the fairest thing is that they all re-establish themselves in the system that they want to go to,” Scott told Today’s Golfer. “They left and gave up those privileges. So, you know, I think they should re-qualify themselves.”

McIlroy said he would like to see the players who left welcomed back through the DP World Tour, playing for their PGA Tour cards as Patrick Reed has this year after he exited LIV in January.

“It would be an amazing thing for this tour if all those guys were funneled through the DP World Tour and were made to qualify that way,” McIlroy said. “I think that’s the right scenario and the right decision and also makes this tour incredibly strong.

“It’s only going to be into the Championship Series. It’s only going to be a handful of cards, so it’s going to be very, very competitive.”

Back in Mexico, Lucas Glover said he’d welcome back guys like Rahm and DeChambeau if they meet the criteria set out by the PGA Tour. But like Scheffler, Glover doesn’t think the path back should come without a payment.

“I do think penalties need to be served,” Glover said. “I don’t know what the stipulations will be. I’m not sure the Tour does, either. I’m not being coy about it. I just don’t know, and I don’t think they do either.”

This week was the first time Rahm has teed it up since he announced his decision to leave LIV. When asked about 2027 and whether he plans to play a full DP World Tour schedule or try to return to the PGA Tour, Rahm said he hadn’t yet engaged the PGA Tour in discussions about his return. He understands that the “Returning Member Program,” which allowed Brooks Koepka to return and which he turned down, is likely not available to him, but he’s willing to pay whatever price commissioner Brian Rolapp sets to return.

“Obviously, Brooks was able to go back through certain circumstances,” Rahm said in Abu Dhabi. “I don’t know if the possibility of that would be open for me or not, but if I have to fulfill a one-year suspension, I think it’s a pretty good position to be and worst-case scenario, I get to play on a wonderful tour for a whole year.

“Most likely, yeah,” Rahm said when asked if he’d take the Koepka deal if it were offered to him now. “Why not? Yeah, but it’s a big if. I seriously doubt I get offered the same deal that Brooks did. But yeah, if I got offered exactly the same penalties as him, I probably would do it, yes.”

Koepka had to make a $5 million charitable donation, forfeit player equity grants on the PGA Tour for five years and was ineligible for sponsor invites to the Signature Events in 2026.

The PGA Tour has not issued a statement since LIV announced it would be winding down, but Rolapp’s previous statements about the issue show he understands the tightrope he will have to walk with a membership that is littered with opinions about the players who left their tour, the value they bring if they return and what a proper punishment should be.

title: 2026 Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship prize money payouts for each DP World Tour player
article_text:
Jon Rahm is back in the winner's circle on the DP World Tour.

The Spaniard won for the 11th time on the circuit Sunday, taking home the title in Abu Dhabi at the 2026 Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship at Yas Links. Rahm finished at 23 under after a closing 67, topping Tyrrell Hatton by two shots and Rory McIlroy by four.

The win was Rahm's first since leaving LIV Golf and his first DP World Tour title since the 2023 Masters.

title: Alex Eala Injury News After Painful Hong Kong Open Final Loss
article_text:
Alex Eala was clearly playing through pain in the women’s singles final at the Hong Kong Open Sunday, but the fast-rising Philippines tennis star did not retire from the match. But she needed to call a medical timeout in the first set while trailing 3-4 in the match she lost in straight sets to Claire Liu.

Eala played on with heavy wrapping on her right leg and fell 3-6, 0-6, ending her season with an injury question that has no public answer yet.

The title match began Sunday, Nov. 8, at Victoria Park Tennis Stadium in Hong Kong, with first serve at 4 p.m. on Centre Court. Eala, the No. 2 seed, arrived ranked No. 17 to Liu’s No. 102. Eala is 21 and left-handed, while Liu is 26 and right-handed. The unseeded American had won four matches without losing a set and was chasing her first WTA title.

“First and foremost, I want to congratulate Claire on an amazing tournament, a great week and a great match. Very, very well deserved and congratulations,” Eala said after the match, as quoted by PhilStar Global. “This season has changed my life. It changed my life for the better. I’m incredibly proud of the work we’ve put in this year. And we’re the only ones who truly know what it took to arrive to this point in our journey.”

Eala had opened well, breaking Liu to love for a 2-1 lead. Liu answered to level at 3-3, then took the lead at 4-3. That is when Eala called for a medical timeout, according to GMA News. She spoke with a trainer, then returned with extra wrapping around her right thigh, just above the knee, according to Tennis Up To Date.

Liu pulled ahead 5-3 with another break, according to the Inquirer, and closed the set 6-3. She then swept the second set, when Eala failed to win a single game.

But despite her obvious pain, Eala never retired. The match ended on court after two sets rather than with a stoppage.

The problem did not surface for the first time Sunday. Eala wore tape on her right knee in her first-round win over Australia’s Emerson Jones, 6-4, 6-3, and afterward she described it as “nothing out of the ordinary” this late in a long season, according to tennis365. She said she felt healthy.

One week earlier, at the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo, Eala took a medical timeout for her ankle during a three-set loss to Diana Shnaider. She finished that match too.

The final was Eala’s last tournament of 2026, according to tennis365, so no match is waiting on her calendar and no scheduled event forces a quick return. The WTA schedule resumes in January, which gives her weeks without matches.

She reached Sunday by working through a heavy week. Eala won tiebreak-heavy matches against Valentova and Ruzic before the semifinal, and she outlasted Maria Sakkari in a rain-soaked semifinal, 7-5, 3-6, 6-4, in a match that ran two hours and 43 minutes, according to Yardbarker. Repeated rain delays stretched the day. Liu, by comparison, beat her semifinal opponent 7-5, 6-4 in one hour and 58 minutes, according to Yardbarker. The tournament director credited Eala’s Filipino fans for near-complete sellouts all week, according to Tennis Tonic.

Eala looked ahead to the final in positive terms, a mindset she tied to the lessons of her whole 2026 season. She said she wanted to “cap it off with a good match, win or lose,” according to tennis365, after her semifinal win over Sakkari. The loss to Liu did not match that hope, but the week still ended with a runner-up finish.

The season itself was a breakthrough. Eala won her first tour title in Washington this year and climbed to a career-high ranking of 17th.

Liu now leads their head-to-head 2-0 after beating Eala in Guangzhou in 2025, where she rallied from a set down.

Whether the knee, the thigh or both need attention is still unanswered, and Eala’s own account of it has yet to come.

title: 6 big names skipping the 2026 DP World Tour Championship (but here's who's in)
article_text:
And then there were 50! Here’s the full DP World Tour Championship field as the 2026 Race to Dubai goes to the wire…

As another season draws to a close, we now know the 50 players that have made it into the 2026 DP World Tour Championship field.

There is, of course, still plenty to play for. Rory McIlroy is searching for a record-breaking eighth Race to Dubai title that will see him overtake Colin Montgomerie for the most Harry Vardon trophies in his cabinet. And, while a host of other players can still get in the mix, including Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship winner Jon Rahm, McIlroy will almost certainly be battling it out with Patrick Reed and Eugenio Chacarra to end the season as Europe’s No.1.

Perhaps more importantly for Reed and Chacarra, though, is the fact that they will end the season with one of the PGA Tour cards that will be dished out to the leading 10 players who otherwise don’t have them for the 2027 season – and there’s a few twists and turns left in that particular race, too.

As well as a total of $10 million up for grabs DP World Tour Championship, there will also be 2,000 Ryder Cup points available as players look to stake a claim in Luke Donald’s team at Adare Manor.

Before we get into it, which players decided to miss the DP World Tour Playoffs altogether?

Who’s skipping the 2026 DP World Tour Championship?

Ten players who finished in the top 70 have decided to give this year’s season-ending Playoffs a miss.

Despite missing Abu Dhabi, Open champion Ryan Fox returns to action having already secured his place in the Dubai finale, but fellow major winners Matt Fitzpatrick (14) and Shane Lowry (20) have decided to steer clear, as have Alex Fitxpatrick (35) and Min Woo Lee (48).

Below the cut-off, Matt Wallace (53) and Ludvig Aberg (54) will also not be in Dubai. The former will stay in the US to concentrate on retaining his PGA Tour card for next year, while the latter had already decided to end his DP World Tour prematurely.

Robert MacIntyre, Si-woo Kim, Justin Rose and Ryan Gerard were among the players who qualified for the Playoffs but chose not to go. The quartet will end the season in 61st, 69th, 75th and 76th respectively.

Among the reasons given include from the older Fitzpatrick, who said he was “uncomfortable” with playing in the Middle East due to the current political climate in the area, and MacIntyre, who expressed similar concerns.

So who is in the 2026 DP World Tour Championship field?

While the DP World Tour Championship field is yet to be finalized, with both Fitzpatricks, Lowry, Lee, Wallace and Aberg all out, it means those in the top 56 will tee up at Jumeirah Golf Estates this week.

This is, of course, subject to change. The reserves will be, in order, Alejandro del Rey, Nathan Kimsey, Michael Hollick, Scott Jamieson and Steffano Mazzoli.

title: Here are the 50 players who qualified for the DP World Tour Championship (and the first 5 out)
article_text:
Eugenio Chacarra, Rory McIlroy and Patrick Reed. That’s where the Race to Dubai list starts. McIlroy jumped Reed via a third-place finish Sunday at the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, but still, these three remain with the best odds of taking home the season-long title when the DP World Tour Championship starts this week at Jumeirah Golf Estates in Dubai.

There can be two winners this week—a tournament winner and a season-long winner. They often are the same, but they certainly can be different.

Chacarra, a 26-year-old from Spain, is on top thanks to three victories this season, two in June and one in October. Reed won twice early in the season, in back-to-back weeks in late January and early February, but has not won since. He tied for 43rd in Abu Dhabi on Sunday. Chacarra tied for 22nd place.

The biggest movers were Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Francesco Laporta. Rahm cruised to a two-shot victory over Hatton in the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship and moved up 45 postions and into sixth place in the standings. Hatton moved up 43 spots to 12th place. Italy's Laporta was tied for the lead with Rahm late Sunday but made a triple-bogey on the 14th hole. He finished in fourth place and moved up 32 spots to 25th place.

“Actually gives me a little extra incentive next week,” Rahm said. “I really didn’t think I was going to have a chance. Those are better odds than I expected.”

There is a $10 million purse on the line with $3 million going to the winner of the tournament. The winner of the Race to Dubai season title will earn a multi-million-dollar bonus from a $6 million purse, which is typically $2 million. McIlroy is looking to win his eighth Race to Dubai title, which would tie Colin Montomgerie, who won what was then called the Order of Merit.
